analysis.one_liner: Reinstate FCC rules requiring internet providers to get consent before selling customers' browsing data.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 18 cosponsors including one Republican, never received a hearing or a vote and died in a House subcommittee at the end of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The FCC had adopted rules in 2016 requiring broadband providers to get customers' permission before using or selling their personal browsing data for advertising. Congress voted in early 2017 to throw those rules out before they took effect, and the President signed that repeal. This bill would have put the same privacy rules back in place by law, so internet providers like Comcast, Verizon, and AT&T could not monetize customers' web history without consent. It was sent to a House subcommittee and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband customers, meaning essentially every American household with home or mobile internet. They would regain control over who can see and sell their browsing history, app usage, and location data.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes all providers of broadband internet access service subject to the FCC's October 27, 2016 privacy order and rules, restoring the protections Congress had just repealed [S2][S3].
Under those rules, internet providers must get customers' affirmative permission (an opt-in) before sharing sensitive personal information such as web browsing history for advertising purposes [S2].
The protections would apply by statute, so they could not be undone again by a simple agency or congressional-review vote as the 2016 rules were [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers — the cable, phone, and wireless companies that carry home internet — would lose a revenue stream from selling or exploiting customer data for targeted advertising, and would face compliance costs. Advertisers who buy that data would also lose access to it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable, phone, and wireless internet providers

drawbacks.text: One legitimate objection raised by broadband companies was that the 2016 rules applied only to internet providers, not to giant web companies like Google and Facebook, which could keep harvesting the same kinds of data without equivalent consent requirements — an uneven playing field (a widely reported industry argument, not stated in the bill).

Providers would bear real compliance costs, and critics argued privacy oversight belonged with the Federal Trade Commission rather than the FCC; the repeal Congress had just passed moved broadband providers to FTC oversight instead (widely reported context).
The bill was a one-section reinstatement of a specific agency order, with no updated negotiation of the privacy standards themselves — supporters accepted the 2016 rules as written [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary people is straightforward control over highly personal data — what websites they visit, where they go — being sold without their knowledge. The costs fall on a small set of large companies, and the strongest objection (asymmetry with big web companies) points to a real gap, but not one that erases the value of the protections. On balance, a consumer win with modest, concentrated costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 4, 2017 by Rep. Jacky Rosen, one day after the President signed a congressional resolution repealing the FCC's 2016 broadband privacy rules before they took effect [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 4 and to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology on April 7, 2017 [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers kept the freedom to use and monetize customers' browsing data without an opt-in consent requirement, since the 2016 FCC rules had already been repealed. Customers gained nothing; the bill never moved.

for.name: Rep. Jacky Rosen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the FCC's 2016 broadband privacy rules by statute [S1][S3].

for.name: Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. and Mike Doyle
for.role: Original cosponsors; Pallone was the ranking Democrat on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Joined Rosen as original cosponsors at introduction [S3].

for.name: 18 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — 17 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Communications and Technology Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

against.name: President Trump
against.what_they_did: The day before this bill was introduced, signed the congressional resolution that repealed the FCC's 2016 broadband privacy rules before they took effect — the action this bill sought to reverse.

against.name: Broadband industry
against.role: Cable, telephone, and wireless internet providers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for the repeal of the 2016 privacy rules the bill sought to restore, and against their reinstatement.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic — 17 of 18 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican — and the Republican-controlled committee took no action; no vote ever occurred to measure the split formally.

industries.industry: Broadband providers (cable, telephone, and wireless internet companies)
industries.note: The bill would bar them from using or selling customers' browsing history, app usage, and location data without opt-in consent, removing a targeted-advertising revenue stream. Their interest in keeping that data freely monetizable runs against customers' privacy.
These firms buy behavioral data derived from internet traffic; restoring the rules would cut off one of the richest data feeds. The public gains privacy at their expense.
